title: Cymbeline
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — Britain. The garden of Cymbeline's palace
about:
Cymbeline is king of Britain. His daughter Imogen has secretly married a worthy but penniless gentleman, Posthumus Leonatus, against her father's wishes. The king's new queen — a stepmother — wants Imogen to marry her own loutish son Cloten instead. Posthumus is banished to Rome. There he falls into a wager with a wily Italian named Iachimo, who bets that he can seduce Imogen. He cannot; he hides in a trunk in her bedroom instead, takes notes on the room, and steals a bracelet to fake the evidence. Posthumus, believing the lie, orders Imogen killed.

The play then opens out into something half-fairy-tale, half-romance. Imogen escapes in boy's clothes. She meets two young woodsmen in a cave in Wales who turn out to be her long-lost brothers, kidnapped in infancy by an exiled lord. She drinks a potion that makes her appear dead. She wakes beside the headless corpse of Cloten, dressed in Posthumus's clothes, and grieves for the wrong man. Meanwhile, a Roman army has invaded Britain over an unpaid tribute. By the end of Act 5, every disguise has been revealed, every family is reunited, and Shakespeare has Jupiter himself descend on an eagle to read out the prophecy that ties the whole knot up.

Shakespeare wrote Cymbeline around 1610, in his last working years, alongside The Winter's Tale and The Tempest. It is the strangest of the late romances — Samuel Johnson called the plot 'unresisting imbecility' — and one of the most affecting. Imogen is widely regarded as one of his finest heroines.

angleCards.title: Imogen.
angleCards.text: Imogen is the heart of the play. She is praised as the most lovable woman in Shakespeare by a long line of readers from Hazlitt to Tennyson, and her scenes with the brothers she does not know are her own carry the play.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Cymbeline as Imogen's play — her marriage, her disguise as a boy, her grief in the wrong man's arms, and her reunions — and see why she has been loved for four hundred years.

angleCards.title: The wager plot.
angleCards.text: Iachimo bets Posthumus he can sleep with Imogen, fakes the evidence, and convinces Posthumus to order her murdered. It is Othello compressed into a single subplot — and the play hands the wronged wife a far better ending.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the wager plot — Iachimo, the trunk, the bracelet, Posthumus's order — as Shakespeare's quieter rewrite of Othello, and watch what he does differently with the same materials.

angleCards.title: A romance, not a tragedy.
angleCards.text: Cymbeline has the bones of three Shakespeare tragedies grafted together — a banished lover, a wager about chastity, a wicked stepmother — and reaches for an ending none of them get. Watch how it earns its happy ending.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Cymbeline as one of the late romances — a play that looks like tragedy and turns it — and see how Shakespeare gets all his characters back into the same room alive.

angleCards.title: The descent of Jupiter.
angleCards.text: Late in the play, Jupiter himself descends from the heavens on an eagle and reads out a prophecy. Some critics think Shakespeare did not write the scene; most now think he did. Either way, it is a god in a machine, used on purpose.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the scene where Jupiter descends on an eagle — is it deliberate magic, theatrical excess, or a deus ex machina Shakespeare is daring us to take seriously?

cast.name: Imogen
cast.description: The princess of Britain and the play's heroine. She marries against her father's wishes, defends her honour against Iachimo, survives her husband's order to kill her, dresses as a boy, finds her lost brothers without knowing them, and pieces the play's family back together in the final scene. Generations of critics have called her Shakespeare's most lovable woman.

cast.name: Posthumus Leonatus
cast.description: A worthy but penniless gentleman, raised at the British court after the death of his father. He has married Imogen in secret and been banished to Rome by her father. He is gullible, brave, devoted, and capable of issuing the worst order a husband can issue. The play forgives him; the audience does so with effort.

cast.name: Cymbeline
cast.description: The old king of Britain, recently remarried to a queen he does not yet realise is a poisoner. He has lost both his sons in infancy and now stands to lose his daughter. He is a figure more bewildered than wicked, kept off the stage for whole acts and ushered back at the end into a kingdom restored by people younger and quicker than he is.

cast.name: Iachimo
cast.description: A Roman gentleman who bets Posthumus he can sleep with Imogen. When he cannot, he hides in a chest in her bedchamber, takes inventory of her body and her room, steals a bracelet, and goes home to convince Posthumus he has slept with her. Iago in a smaller theatre, with a smaller stake and, mercifully, a quieter conscience.

cast.name: The Queen
cast.description: Imogen's stepmother, who has fed the king poison for years and wants her son Cloten to marry Imogen and inherit the throne. Shakespeare's most undisguised wicked queen. She dies offstage in Act 5 confessing all of it, in a final speech reported rather than performed.

cast.name: Belarius
cast.description: A lord wrongly banished by Cymbeline twenty years ago who has been raising the king's two stolen sons in a cave in Wales under false names. He is the play's link between the lost family and the rediscovered one, and the gentle Welsh court that turns the play's second half toward romance.

acclaim.quote: Imogen is the perfection of female loveliness.
Of all Shakespeare's pictures of female perfection, Imogen is the most attractive.

whyItMatters.title: Imogen
whyItMatters.body: Imogen has been the favourite Shakespeare heroine of several centuries of readers — Hazlitt, Tennyson, Swinburne, Shaw — and it is not hard to see why. She is the only Shakespeare heroine who marries early in the play and spends the rest of it married to the wrong opinion her husband has of her. She is the only one who has to deliver a soliloquy about her own death sentence at the hands of the man she loves. She is the only one who wakes from a sleeping potion next to a headless corpse and grieves over the body, mistakenly, as her husband's. She is the only one who finds her own brothers after a lifetime apart without realising who they are. She is also the only one who does all of this disguised as a boy in the Welsh mountains. Shakespeare gives her more situations than any of his other heroines and lets her come out of all of them with her dignity intact. The play has been argued over for everything — its tone, its plot, its god from the machine — but no one has ever argued about Imogen.

whyItMatters.title: Shakespeare Rewriting Himself
whyItMatters.body: Cymbeline is one of Shakespeare's late plays, written after the four great tragedies, and it reads as a man rewriting his own earlier work. The wager plot — a man tricked into believing his wife unfaithful, issuing an order for her death — is the spine of Othello. Posthumus is a younger, gentler Othello; Iachimo is Iago dialled down two notches and given a conscience; Imogen is the Desdemona who lives, escapes, and meets her husband again. Shakespeare wrote both plays. He wrote them seven years apart. He knew exactly what he was doing when he sent the same dramatic situation through the romance mode instead of the tragic one and let everyone survive. Cymbeline is not less serious than Othello; it is, in its own way, an answer. The same materials, handled in this register, give the wronged wife back her life. The play is the place where Shakespeare, in his last working years, tests whether his own deepest tragic plot can be made to bend the other way.

whyItMatters.title: Jupiter on an Eagle
whyItMatters.body: Late in Act 5, after the war between Rome and Britain has been resolved and most of the disguises have been worked out, Posthumus falls asleep in prison and Shakespeare sends a god down on stage. Jupiter descends sitting on the back of an eagle, surrounded by the ghosts of Posthumus's dead family, reads out a prophecy on a tablet, blesses Posthumus, and ascends again. It is the most flagrant deus ex machina in Shakespeare. Editors for two centuries have suspected the scene is not his — too theatrical, too crude, too literally machine-driven. Modern scholarship has come round to thinking it probably is his after all, and that he meant the descent of the god to feel exactly as artificial as it feels: a deliberate, late-career move into the territory of masque and romance, where the rules of the tragic stage no longer apply and the audience is asked to accept rescue from above. The scene divides audiences exactly as Shakespeare seems to have wanted it to: some find it absurd, some moving, some both. It is the moment Cymbeline announces that this is a play in which problems can be solved from outside — and dares its audience to believe it.
